archetype.name: Improviser (now accuracy-first)
archetype.definition: A third-year passer who still holds the ball and creates outside the pocket with his legs, but who this season has paired that with on-time, accurate throws underneath and big chunk plays between 10 and 20 yards.

report.headline: The accuracy leap looks real; the sacks and the Seattle test are the catch.
report.take:
Williams has played only four games, missing three starts while Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent filled in, and in them he has been a different passer from the one in his first two seasons. His 0.307 EPA per dropback ranks 5th of 45, his 8.25 CPOE ranks 2nd, and his 71% completion rate ranks 4th. Last year he completed 58.1% with a -3.5 CPOE. That is not a hot week. It is a change in kind, and the charting supports it: his bad-throw rate has fallen from 17.8% to 11.3%. The ball is going where it should.

The shape of the offense explains part of it. Ben Johnson's group leans run (pass rate over expected -2.6, 20th), and Williams's intended air yards of 6.23 sit well short of the sticks (-3.56). More than two-thirds of his charted throws travel under 10 yards, and he completes 80.2% of them. The damage comes when he does push it: 0.735 EPA per attempt on throws of 10-plus yards and 0.811 in the 10-19 range, with Rome Odunze at 1.113 EPA per target and Luther Burden at 0.668. It is a quick-game base that sets up intermediate shots, and he is hitting both.

The numbers hide two things. First, the old flaw is back. He has taken 12 sacks for an 8.8% rate (36th of 45), and 30.8% of his pressures end in sacks, a long way from last year's top-five 15.9% and closer to his rookie habit. His 3.22-second time to throw is basically last season's, so this is not a new holding problem. It is the cost of an extender's style, and his 14 scrambles at 0.752 EPA with 7 first downs mostly pay for it. His designed runs (-0.802 EPA, 62.5% stuffed) do not. Second, the season line is front-loaded. Week 1's 59-37 shootout at Carolina produced 18.6 EPA and both rushing touchdowns. In Week 2 against Minnesota, now the top-ranked defense, he managed -1.0 EPA and 138 yards while under pressure on 40.6% of dropbacks.

The two games since his return, against mid-pack defenses Atlanta and New England, were both clearly positive, at 10.6 and 13.6 EPA. Even with the Minnesota dud included, his last three run at 0.22 EPA per dropback, still well above the 0.04 league average. The open question is what happens against elite defensive fronts, and Seattle, second in defensive EPA, is the next one to answer it.

strengths.title: Accuracy jump backed by charting
strengths.body: His CPOE has climbed by 11.8 points from last season, and the drop in bad throws shows it is not just catchable short targets padding the number. Some of it is scheme, with more quick, defined throws. But he has also posted +8.5 CPOE at 10-19 yards and +21.3 deep on small samples. Expect some cooling from a #2 rank, though not a return to last year's 58%.

strengths.title: Intermediate throws carry the offense
strengths.body: Only 25 of his throws have landed in the 10-19 yard window, yet they have added 20.3 EPA, more than his 60 short throws. Odunze and Burden are winning there, and the run-leaning base keeps those windows open. The per-play rate will come down on more volume, but the profile is sound.

strengths.title: Scrambles that move chains
strengths.body: When the play breaks, his legs turn it into profit: 0.752 EPA per scramble, with half of his scrambles earning a first down. This has been part of him all along (7th in rushing yards both prior seasons), so it is durable. It is also the main reason his sacks are a tolerable trade rather than a fatal one.

concerns.title: Sacks are back to rookie-ish levels
concerns.body: He ranks 36th of 45 in sack rate, which works out to a 51-sack pace over 17 games. His pressure-to-sack rate has slid from last year's top-five mark toward the middle of the pack. Part of this is the price of extending plays at a 3.22-second release. Part is pass protection: a 40.6% pressure rate against Minnesota turned into a lost game. Against good fronts this is the issue that decides his day.

concerns.title: Elite-defense sample is one dud
concerns.body: His only game against a top-five defense was the 9-3 loss to Minnesota: 138 yards, -1.0 EPA, -5.6 CPOE. One game is a hint, not a verdict. But the other three opponents rank 13th, 16th and 19th in defensive EPA, so the season efficiency has not yet been tested against a front like Seattle's.

concerns.title: Touchdowns lag the efficiency
concerns.body: A 4% TD rate (27th) does not match a top-five EPA passer. Red-zone success of 0.40 on 20 plays and a run-leaning offense both cap scoring passes. This is more likely noise and play-calling than a skill gap, so modest upward drift is the expectation, not a surge.

trend.note: Outside the Week 2 Minnesota game, every start has been strongly positive, and the two games since his return (10.6 and 13.6 EPA) look like a stable level. His last three sit a bit below his season rate only because Week 1's shootout is out of the window.

nextGame.headline: Toughest defense since Minnesota, but with soft underneath spots
nextGame.body:
Seattle grades 2nd in defensive EPA and 3rd against the pass. It has allowed the fewest passing yards a game to quarterbacks (176.1) and the second-fewest fantasy points. It is also the best in the league at stopping explosive and deep passes, which is exactly where Williams's biggest plays come from. The opening is underneath: Seattle ranks only 21st in short-pass EPA, and Williams completes 80.2% of his throws under 10 yards. Expect a dink-and-move game plan. His day hinges on whether the line holds against a defense that ranks 3rd in hit rate, after Minnesota's pressure sank him in Week 2.

Availability tilts both ways. Seattle is without linebacker Drake Thomas (87% of snaps), which should loosen the middle for Colston Loveland, who becomes the clear tight end with Cole Kmet on injured reserve. D'Andre Swift should carry a bigger load with Kyle Monangai out, a steady checkdown outlet against a defense that has held lead backs under their averages. On the other side, Seattle's offense ranks 25th in EPA and 29th rushing. It is missing quarterback Drew Lock, and left tackle Charles Cross is doubtful. Chicago's 3rd-ranked sack rate could win field position and keep this a low-total grind (46.5, Bears +3). That helps the Bears' chances more than Williams's volume. Williams himself practiced fully and is active.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs Seattle's soft spot
keyMatchups.body: Seattle shuts down deep throws but gives up EPA on short ones. That fits Williams's quick-game base and his strong short-throw efficiency. Yards after the catch from Burden, Loveland and Swift likely decide whether Chicago moves the ball.

keyMatchups.title: Intermediate shots vs best explosive defense
keyMatchups.body: His EPA lives on 10-plus air-yard throws, and Seattle allows the lowest explosive-pass rate and the best deep EPA in the league. Expect fewer chunk plays than usual. One or two hits to Odunze could swing the game.

keyMatchups.title: Pressure vs a ball-holder
keyMatchups.body: Seattle ranks 3rd in hit rate, and Williams already takes sacks at a bottom-tier rate while holding the ball over three seconds. If he turns pressure into scrambles rather than sacks, his floor holds. If not, Week 2 is the template.

nextGame.watch: How quickly he gets the ball out on early downs: a sub-3-second rhythm against Seattle's pressure is the tell that the accuracy leap travels against elite defenses.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy gain looks structural: fewer bad throws, a cleaner quick game and receivers winning at intermediate depth. It should keep him among the more efficient passers even as the CPOE cools from 2nd in the league. I project 230-270 passing yards a game with 1.2-1.8 touchdown passes, the latter a touch above his current rate as red-zone luck evens out. His per-dropback EPA should settle around 0.12-0.22, still well above the league's 0.04. What will regress is the 0.811 EPA rate on intermediate throws and the Week 1-fueled rushing line. Expect 18-30 rushing yards a game, coming mostly from scrambles, not designed runs.

The swing variable is protection. His sack rate is the one number that has moved the wrong way from last year, and it showed up in the one game against an elite front. In a run-leaning offense, volume will not rescue a bad day, so his weekly range against top defenses will be wider than his season line suggests.
swingFactors: Whether the CPOE gains hold against top defenses
Red-zone touchdown conversion in a run-leaning offense

confidence.note: Only four games and 150 dropbacks, with one against an elite defense, but the accuracy gain is backed by charting.
